newsitem.title: THAILAND: IBM investment boosts growing Thai electronics.
newsitem.headline: IBM investment boosts growing Thai electronics.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp's planned $594 million investment in two hard disk drive plants in Thailand would boost the country's fast growing electronics industry, analysts said on Thursday.

IBM on Wednesday won tax incentive privileges from Thailand's Board of Investment (BoI) for its plants in eastern Chonburi and Prachinburi provinces that would produce about 14.1 million disk drives a year from late 1997.
An IBM representative in Bangkok said: "The plants will produce drives with latest technology and will employ about 6,700 workers."
He said the plants would export more than 80 percent of their output, earning Thailand about $1.8 billion in foreign exchange a year when they ran at full capacity.
Stock market analysts said the IBM plants would benefit Thai-based computer parts producers listed on the Thai bourse, including KR Precision Plc and Hana Micro Electronics Plc.

"Companies like KR Precision would benefit from the IBM projects in the long run when their capacities are expanded to meet demands of both IBM and current parts buyers like Seagate," a foreign analyst at a Thai brokerage firm said.
The IBM plants are not the biggest computer components projects hosted by Thailand.
Texas Instruments Inc $1.2 billion Thai semiconductor joint venture is scheduled to start production of advanced memory chips from the third quarter of 1997.
Seagate Technology Inc, the world's largest independent producer of hard drives, currently employs nearly 40,000 workers at its Thai plants, making it one of Thailand's biggest employers.

Minebea Co Ltd, the world's biggest producer of miniature ball bearings and other high-precision computer parts, has invested about $1.35 billion in land and factories of its eight wholly owned subsidiaries in Thailand since 1982.
Electronics has been Thailand's fastest growing industry over the past few years.
The commerce ministry said exports of electronic circuit boards and parts rose 28.5 percent to about $2.32 billion in 1995, against $1.02 billion earned by the sector in 1991.

BoI deputy secretary general Chakramon Phasukvanich said, however, that the Thai electronics industry and the country's role as a production base for medium-end computer parts had been hurt by absence of local support industries.
He said 80 percent of components and parts used by the Thai electronics industry were imports from other countries.

Samrit Ruengwattanaporn, Seagate Technology's senior purchasing manager, said his firm needed to import about 90 percent of parts and materials for its Thai manufactured products, including 200,000 pairs of surgical gloves a month, mostly from Singapore.
